pr_title: Improve documentation and error messaging for local extension installations without executables
pr_body:
Fixes #9760 

## Requirements

> ### Acceptance Criteria
> 
> **Given** I am in a directory that doesn't have an executable for `gh` to call as an extension
> **When** I run `gh extension install .`
> **Then** I get an informative message on stderr saying "An extension has been installed but there is no executable found in this directory, perhaps you need to build it?"
> 
> This should be styled when there is a TTY and unstyled when there is not.
> 
> **When** I run `gh extension install --help`
> **Then** I see an explanation that `gh extension install .` creates a symlink to an executable in the local directory regardless of whether it exists or not, and it's necessary for the user to build executables out of band if need be.

## Demo

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/3c7e411a-d331-4959-9850-22e4dea78d6d)

## Reproduction

**Error message:**

```shell
# Setup path to `gh` binary built from this PR
bingh="<PATH_TO_GH_BINARY>"

$bingh ext create testing-9933
cd gh-testing-9933
rm gh-testing-9933
$bingh ext install .
```

**Cleanup/reset:**

```shell
# Assuming you're still in the testing extension dir...
cd ..
$bingh ext remove gh-testing-9933
rm -rf gh-testing-9933
```
pr_comments:
It occurs to me that this is a breaking change. I wonder if there are scripts out there that do:

```
gh ext install .
go build ...
```

Which will start breaking. Need to think about this.

So we have two options here:
 1. We just ship this and if someone complains we either say "sorry" and revert it, or say "sorry" and they hopefully make an easy change to their script
 2. We only show this message in interactive mode, which is probably the most common

The advantage of not breaking is clear, the advantage of breaking is consistency. I'd probably favour consistency and if it breaks someone we can apologise. Happy for someone to disagree though.

> It occurs to me that this is a breaking change. I wonder if there are scripts out there that do:
> 
> ```
> gh ext install .
> go build ...
> ```
> 
> Which will start breaking. Need to think about this.

@williammartin could you talk more about why this would be breaking? Apologies if it is obvious 😅 

Are you talking about if someone had a script checking if `gh ext install .` is successful, then it's no longer going to be successful because we're sending a message out on stderr?

Maybe we only send that message to stderr when there is a TTY?

@BagToad my bad, I actually thought this was erroring (exit non-zero), not just a warning. I don't feel strongly either way about just the message. Maybe I'd favour just having it on TTY, since realistically, people who are running it in a script probably understand what the semantics are of the command.

@williammartin, I think you're right actually. We are returning an `error` now and that makes us exit non-zero:

```
! an extension has been installed but there is no executable: expected executable file named "gh-testing-9933" in /Users/kynanware/Documents/orgs/cli/gh-testing-9933, perhaps you need to build it?

❯ echo $?
1
```

Ideas:

- Only return the error on TTY, so we only exit non-zero with a TTY. 
    - I think this one is a bit confusing - I don't like having a different exit code whether there is a TTY or not.  
- We do not print this message to stderr or return an err like originally written in the A/C. Instead, we print it to stdout when there is a TTY. Exit code remains zero for this case.
I think we should continue to exit 0 in all cases. I think most uses of `cs.WarningIcon()` (which is the icon for `!`) go to ErrOut. I'd probably be inclined to continue sending it to that stream.

Thanks @williammartin 🙇 

I pushed a few commits to fix that if you could give it another review, please. 

I also added tests in `command_test.go` to demonstrate this additional behavior.

## Demo

No TTY
```
❯ $bingh ext install . | cat    

❯ echo $?
0
```

With TTY

```
❯ $bingh ext install .          
! an extension has been installed but there is no executable: executable file named "gh-testing-9933" in /Users/kynanware/Documents/orgs/cli/gh-testing-9933 is required to run the extension after install. Perhaps you need to build it?

❯ echo $?
0
```

### Comments:

I saw inconsistency in the way the rest of the codebase checks if we are in a TTY before printing to stderr. I saw three different approaches:

**1. Check if stderr is TTY only, then print to stderr:**

https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/9177b22a213318ccc00a9b08fbac1dd14fb3a839/pkg/cmd/gist/view/view.go#L108-L110

**2. Check if stdout is TTY only, then print to stderr:**

https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/9177b22a213318ccc00a9b08fbac1dd14fb3a839/pkg/cmd/extension/command.go#L168-L170

**3. Check if both stdout and stderr are TTY, then print to stderr:**

https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/9177b22a213318ccc00a9b08fbac1dd14fb3a839/pkg/cmd/repo/fork/fork.go#L187
https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/9177b22a213318ccc00a9b08fbac1dd14fb3a839/pkg/cmd/repo/fork/fork.go#L213-L218

---

With all the different options, I chose option _2 - check if stdout is TTY only, then print to stderr_ because there is precedent for this already in `extension/command.go` (see example linked in point 2 above 👆 ). Snippet of what I proposed:

https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/e5eedefd093afa784d5f39323be31916738d02a3/pkg/cmd/extension/command.go#L344-L346

Let me know if you think I should have chosen a different option, please.

After some discussion we decided that the message should only be displayed when there is a TTY.

 ### Acceptance Criteria

**Given** I invoke `gh` without a TTY
**And Given** I am in a directory that doesn't have an executable for `gh` to call as an extension
**When** I run `gh extension install .`
**Then** I get no output (as is current behaviour)

```
~/workspace/cli/bin/gh ext install . | cat
```

**Given** I invoke `gh` with a TTY
**And Given** I am in a directory that doesn't have an executable for `gh` to call as an extension
**When** I run `gh extension install .`
**Then** I get an informative message on stderr saying "An extension has been installed but there is no executable found in this directory, perhaps you need to build it?"

```
➜ ~/workspace/cli/bin/gh ext install .
! an extension has been installed but there is no executable: executable file named "gh-local" in /Users/williammartin/workspace/cli-triaging/local-ext/gh-local is required to run the extension after install. Perhaps you need to build it?
```

This should be styled when there is a TTY and unstyled when there is not.

**When** I run `gh extension install --help`
 **Then** I see an explanation that `gh extension install .` creates a symlink to an executable in the local directory regardless of whether it exists or not, and it's necessary for the user to build executables out of band if need be.

```
➜  gh-local ~/workspace/cli/bin/gh  extension install --help
Install a GitHub CLI extension from a GitHub or local repository.

For GitHub repositories, the repository argument can be specified in `OWNER/REPO` format or as a full repository URL.
The URL format is useful when the repository is not hosted on github.com.

For local repositories, often used while developing extensions, use `.` as the
value of the repository argument. Note the following:

- After installing an extension from a locally cloned repository, the GitHub CLI will
manage this extension as a symbolic link (or equivalent mechanism on Windows) pointing
to an executable file with the same name as the repository in the repository's root.
For example, if the repository is named `gh-foobar`, the symbolic link will point
to `gh-foobar` in the extension repository's root.
- When executing the extension, the GitHub CLI will run the executable file found
by following the symbolic link. If no executable file is found, the extension
will fail to execute.
- If the extension is precompiled, the executable file must be built manually and placed
in the repository's root.

For the list of available extensions, see <https://github.com/topics/gh-extension>.
```

LGTM

issue_context.title: Broken installation of extension in development
issue_context.body:
### Describe the bug

I tried installing extension in development from a local folder and while extension appears installed according to the `list` command, it is not executable. 

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

0. Checkout https://github.com/IvanRibakov/gh-workflow-stats and navigate to the repo root
1. Install extension from local folder: `gh extensions install .`
2. Check that extension appears installed: `gh ext list`
3. Invoke installed extension: `gh workflow-stats -h`

### Expected vs actual behavior

Expecting extension in development installed from a local folder to be usable as if it was installed from Github repo tagged release, instead getting a broken installation that is unusable.

### Logs

```
$ pwd
<some-path>/gh-workflow-stats

$ git status
On branch feature/filter_multiple_statuses
Your branch is up to date with 'origin/feature/filter_multiple_statuses'.

nothing to commit, working tree clean

$ gh ext list
no installed extensions found

$ GH_DEBUG=true gh extensions install .

$ gh ext list
NAME               REPO  VERSION
gh workflow-stats        

$ gh workflow-stats -h
failed to run extension: fork/exec /home/ivan/.local/share/gh/extensions/gh-workflow-stats/gh-workflow-stats: no such file or directory

$ ls -la /home/ivan/.local/share/gh/extensions/gh-workflow-stats
lrwxrwxrwx 1 ivan ivan 47 Oct 15 13:26 /home/ivan/.local/share/gh/extensions/gh-workflow-stats -> <some-path>/gh-workflow-stats
```
comments:
Hey @IvanRibakov,

Thanks for the bug report. I'll admit firstly that I don't have much experience with the `extension` command (so it may take me a moment to work through your other issue).

This seems to be the [expected behaviour](https://github.com/cli/cli/issues/4194#issuecomment-910308364) from when binary support was added to extensions. Under the covers a `gh extension install .` is just creating a symlink from the extensions dir (which is why it appears in `ext list`), to a file in the `.` directory.

The expectation is that you build the extension locally using whatever toolchain is required, since `gh` can't really do that for you.

However, it really seems like we should have a more useful error message than this, (perhaps on `ext install .`, though that might be a breaking change for someone) and to add something to the help text to indicate this requirement. What do you think?

Hi @williammartin, thanks for the pointer to the comment. Building the binary locally seems to have sorted out the issue for me.

 > However, it really seems like we should have a more useful error message than this, (perhaps on ext install ., though that might be a breaking change for someone) and to add something to the help text to indicate this requirement.

That certainly sounds like an improvement. 

What I think would have helped me personally save a lot of time here (and also with the [other issue](https://github.com/cli/cli/issues/9759) I created earlier today) is some sort of mention of the custom workflow that comes with the binary support in the [main Github CLI app documentation/manual](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_extension_install).

> The expectation is that you build the extension locally using whatever toolchain is required, since gh can't really do that for you.

Fair enough, and I can see how this is something that a person creating a new extension from scratch would probably have thought about before and is aware of. I just wish this was made a bit more transparent / easier to find.
Do you mind if I reopen this issue to track some changes we'd like to see? It seems like some changes here would be valuable and it's nice to have this issue as the direct reference.

@IvanRibakov thinking about this more, I think the best place for us to inform the user about this is on `gh extension install .`

We can then issue a warning that they've installed an extension but there was no executable to target yet, so they probably need to build one.

### Acceptance Criteria

**Given** I am in a directory that doesn't have an executable for `gh` to call as an extension
**When** I run `gh extension install .`
**Then** I get an informative message on stderr saying "An extension has been installed but there is no executable found in this directory, perhaps you need to build it?"

This should be styled when there is a TTY and unstyled when there is not.

**When** I run `gh extension install --help`
**Then** I see an explanation that `gh extension install .` creates a symlink to an executable in the local directory regardless of whether it exists or not, and it's necessary for the user to build executables out of band if need be.

review_comments:
I don't think there's anything that requires the local directory to be a repository, so this doesn't seem quite right.

That said I understand that the short and use indicate that it's a repository, so let's just leave it alone.

I had this thought too and here is how I rationalized it to myself:

I saw us using `repository` to describe the directory as a suggestion that we want extension authors to consider their extensions as repositories, even if we don't strictly require it. We especially want them to consider them as _GitHub_ repositories, except in this case it is cloned locally.

Maybe there's holes on my logic 🤪 , but that was my thoughts and why I didn't change it.

I'll mark this thread as resolved, but feel free to re-open it if you think we have something to do here 🙏
This isn't the only reason that `err` might occur, so if we want to be specific, we should check [`os.IsNotExist`](https://pkg.go.dev/os#IsNotExist).
Do you think it's worth doc-ing how this is different on windows?

@jtmcg and I [also wondered about that](https://github.com/cli/cli/pull/9933#discussion_r1847049096) but landed on it being an implementation detail that may confuse the docs if we try to document it. 

What do you think?
@williammartin and I talked about this and decided to add a hint to the help text without fully documenting the differences.
